findings.title: The named referent against human-assigned names
findings.claim: The opening name can also be heard as identifying a referent distinct from names people assign to objects of worship: 12:40 contrasts humanly assigned names without revealed authority with Allah as the sole ruler and object of worship, while 19:65 asks whether anyone is His namesake.
findings.mechanism: The focus carrier is ismi, the noun that identifies a referent, beside Allah as the named one. In 12:40, أسماء سميتموها supplies the independent human act of naming and says no authority was sent down for those names; the same ayah says judgment belongs only to Allah and commands worship of Him alone. In 19:65, the question هل تعلم له سميا tests whether anyone is a namesake or equal. Those contacts make the focus's named Allah legible against both humanly conferred labels and a possible namesake.
findings.reader_payoff: The basmala's name is more than an empty label: the wider wording points it toward a distinctive referent whose authority and worship are not assigned by people.
findings.containment: The focus remains an invocation in the name of Allah. This does not turn the proper name into a common noun, make authority a dictionary meaning of ismi, or claim that 89:0 itself states the later verses' exclusive-worship relation. The namesake contact follows the packet's supplied facet; سميا also permits an equality reading.

epistemic.reason: The focus forms and both target ayah texts are supplied, but the connection records are nominations, target morphology and explicit source-trust labels are absent, and the synthesis is a contextual inference.

branch_activations.carrier: The focus's ism is the identifying noun in the construction, attached to Allah.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 12:40 contrasts names people assigned to rivals with Allah's authority; 19:65 asks whether anyone is a namesake or equal to Him.
branch_activations.activation: The human naming contrast and the namesake question meet the focus's identifying-name carrier, making its referent legible against labels and equivalents supplied by the wider text.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus's name identifies a distinctive referent rather than one humanly assigned label among others.
branch_activations.boundary: This is a contextual naming relation; it does not claim that the word ism itself means authority or that its form alone asserts uniqueness.

branch_activations.boundary: The branch excludes bare proper-name uses; here its object role is retained only as a contextual relation, while the focus's proper-name form remains intact.

findings.title: The name as an active orientation
findings.claim: The opening can also be heard as an active orientation through a name: elsewhere that name is remembered in devotion, mentioned over an act of eating, and the full formula accompanies a statement introduced as from Solomon.
findings.mechanism: The focus binds the preposition bi to ism and the name Allah. In 73:8, the Lord's name is the object of remembrance beside an instruction to devote oneself to Him; 6:118 says to eat from what Allah's name was mentioned over; 27:30 places the exact full basmala in a statement introduced as from Solomon. These independent uses meet the focus's name carrier and its open prepositional relation, showing the name as something that can frame utterance and deed.
findings.reader_payoff: The basmala is perceptible as more than an identifying label: its naming can orient what is said or undertaken toward the one named.
findings.containment: The focus still says in/by the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Merciful. The other verses show supplied uses of the name and formula; they do not make this focus mention food, a letter, or a specific action.

epistemic.reason: The packet supplies exact target Arabic and the focus surface, but these are reciprocal nominations without target morphology or explicit source-trust labels; the common action-framing relation is an inference across contexts.

branch_activations.carrier: Ism is the identifying noun in the focus; the attached Allah names its referent.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 73:8 commands remembrance of the Lord's name and devotion; 6:118 places mention of Allah's name over food before eating; 27:30 uses the full basmala in a statement introduced as from Solomon.
branch_activations.activation: The focus's identifying name meets separate remembrance, eating, and communication acts in the wider text. Their contact makes the focus's prepositional name phrase available as an orientation that accompanies what is said or done.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The opening name can frame a subsequent utterance or deed in relation to Allah, rather than functioning only as a detached label.
branch_activations.boundary: The focus does not specify any of those external acts. This is a contextual use pattern, not a claim that one particular act is grammatically present in 89:0.

findings.title: Mercy with wide reach and particular enactment
findings.claim: The focus's paired mercy names can be heard with both wide reach and a particular form of enactment: 7:156 says God's mercy encompasses everything, then speaks of writing it for those described there.
findings.mechanism: The focus's two mercy epithets carry the root's active sense of protecting and doing good. The independent wording in 7:156 says وَرَحْمَتِي وَسِعَتْ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ and then فَسَأَكْتُبُهَا لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ..., so the wide scope of mercy stands beside a specified act of its being written for a described group. That contact makes breadth and particular enactment perceptible together.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hold the reach of mercy and its directed enactment together without treating all outcomes as identical.
findings.containment: This wider verse contextualizes the focus; it does not lexically define either epithet or restrict the focus's mercy to the group named in 7:156. Its distinction is between the stated scope of mercy and the particular promise in that verse.

epistemic.reason: The exact focus and target wording and a matching focus-root branch are supplied. The cross-ayah relation is interpretive, and the connection is a nomination without target morphology or explicit source-trust labels.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Bu iç yöneliş, acınan kişiyi esirgemeyi ve ona iyilikte bulunmayı gerektiren etkin bir sonuç taşır.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus's al-Rahman and al-Rahim carry mercy as an orientation that reaches protection and good.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 7:156 says that God's mercy encompasses everything and then says it will be written for those described in the verse.
branch_activations.activation: The independent statement of all-encompassing mercy and its particular inscription contacts the focus's active mercy sense, making scope and enactment a joint reading.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus's mercy can be heard as broadly reaching while also taking particular form in the wider verse.
branch_activations.boundary: The target verse supplies the scope and promised inscription; this does not make those details part of the focus's lexical definition.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Tanrı hakkında kullanıldığında esirgemenin genişliği ve yaratılmışlara iyilik olarak ulaşması belirginleşir.
branch_activations.carrier: Both mercy epithets describe Allah in the focus.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: The target explicitly gives God's mercy the scope كل شيء before describing its inscription for a specified group.
branch_activations.activation: The target's scope phrase meets the focus's divine-use facet, adding a concrete wider statement of reach while preserving the later particular promise.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: Divine mercy is available here as both wide in reach and specifically enacted.
branch_activations.boundary: The target does not establish identical outcomes for every being, and its later recipient clause does not cancel its stated breadth.

findings.title: Mercy reaching kinship and pardon
findings.claim: The opening's mercy names can also be heard in a social register: 24:22 places giving to close relatives beside pardon and then calls Allah forgiving and merciful.
findings.mechanism: The focus's al-Rahman and al-Rahim carry the compassion-and-protective-good branch. In 24:22, the independent context names close relatives among those to receive, commands pardon and forbearance, and closes with وَاللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ. The care and kinship relation meets the focus's mercy carriers, allowing its compassion to be heard as something that reaches human bonds and action.
findings.reader_payoff: The mercy named in the focus becomes concrete in care for relatives and others in need, and in the act of forgiving; the kinship branch supplies a relational dimension without replacing the plain mercy sense.
findings.containment: The focus attributes mercy to Allah. 24:22 supplies human kinship and care as context; this does not call Allah a relative and does not make al-Rahman or al-Rahim mean kinship or womb.

epistemic.reason: The exact focus and target Arabic and relevant focus-root branches are present. The connection nomination supplies no target morphology or explicit trust label, so the kinship relation remains a contextual inference.

branch_activations.independent_trigger: 24:22 urges giving to close relatives, the needy, and migrants and says وليعفوا وليصفحوا, let them pardon and overlook.
branch_activations.activation: The target's acts of giving, pardoning, and overlooking meet the focus's active mercy facet, showing one wider way compassion reaches people.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The mercy named in the focus can be heard as compassion that reaches material care and forbearance.
branch_activations.boundary: The actions belong to the wider verse and illustrate a contextual relation; they are not additional clauses in 89:0.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Ortak soydan gelme, kişiler arasında yakın ve kalıcı bir soy ilişkisi kurar.
branch_activations.carrier: The focus's mercy epithets carry the same supplied root whose branch includes close kinship.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: 24:22 explicitly names أولي القربى, close relatives, as recipients of giving and places that care beside the mercy name al-Rahim.
branch_activations.activation: The target's close-kin relation independently activates a kinship register around the focus's mercy words, which return through the shared root and the target's closing al-Rahim.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus's mercy remains compassion, with close kinship available as one concrete relational field in which the wider text places it.
branch_activations.boundary: This is a contextual kinship resonance, not a lexical claim that either focus epithet means blood relation, and not a claim of kinship between Allah and people.
